rows: Employers must ensure employees can receive immediate help if injured or taken ill at work.
First-aid duties apply to every workplace and to self-employed work.
Workplaces need a suitably stocked first-aid kit.
An appointed person or people must take charge of first-aid arrangements.
Employees must be told about the first-aid arrangements.
First-aid needs assessment should reflect hazards, workforce and work patterns.
Training level should match the first-aid needs assessment.
Arrangements should account for remote, home, shared or co-working environments where relevant.
HSE guidance does not prescribe one universal kit or fixed number of first-aiders for every workplace.
Suitability depends on workforce size, hazards, shifts, remoteness and access to emergency services.
Gas safety duties cover employers, domestic consumers, landlords and the gas supply industry.
Work on gas appliances and fittings must be carried out by appropriately registered and competent engineers where required.
Employers must manage gas fittings and work activities so they do not put workers or the public at risk.
Landlord duties include maintenance, safety checks and record keeping for relevant gas installations.
Unsafe gas work can create fire, explosion and carbon-monoxide risks.
Appliances, flues and pipework should be installed and maintained safely.
Safety defects identified during checks require prompt corrective action.
HSE guidance distinguishes appliance work from non-gas wet work.
General guidance does not confirm that a particular appliance, flue or installation is safe.
Legal responsibility and check requirements depend on tenure, ownership, appliance provision and installation type.
Food businesses must provide accurate allergen information for the food they sell.
Guidance covers allergen information and best practice for handling allergens.
Controls should address ingredient information and cross-contamination risk.
Written allergen information is encouraged in the out-of-home sector alongside staff conversation.
Managers, kitchen staff and front-of-house staff need coordinated allergen procedures.
Changes to ingredients or suppliers require allergen information to be reviewed.
Training and checklists support consistent allergen communication.
Food businesses should have procedures for responding to customer allergy questions.
Guidance compliance cannot be inferred from the type or location of a premises.
Actual allergen safety depends on current ingredients, recipes, supplier data, staff practice and cross-contact controls.
Safety data sheets describe chemical hazards and provide handling, storage and emergency information.
Suppliers must provide an up-to-date safety data sheet for substances dangerous for supply where the law requires it.
Safety data sheets help users prepare a workplace risk assessment.
A safety data sheet is not itself a risk assessment.
Workplace exposure limits are used when assessing and controlling inhalation exposure.
Control guidance sheets provide task-oriented advice for hazardous substances.
Exposure controls must be selected for the substance, process and route of exposure.
Health surveillance may be needed where there is an identifiable disease or adverse health effect linked to exposure.
A supplier data sheet cannot verify actual exposure or control performance at a workplace.
Exposure limits and surveillance requirements must be applied with task-specific measurements and competent interpretation.
